content: Ichthyosis refers to a group of genetic dermatological disorders that affect both humans and domestic animals. Individuals or animals with ichthyosis exhibit scaly skin, which can resemble the appearance of fish scales. The term ichthyosis is derived from the Greek word ιχθύωσις, which translates to forming fish, reflecting the scaly skin characteristic of the condition. Historically, ichthyosis was sometimes referred to as pseudo-leprosy due to its superficial resemblance to leprosy. The term is also occasionally used to describe a specific subtype, ichthyosis vulgaris. Ichthyosis can be classified into congenital and acquired forms. While ichthyosis acquisita is acquired, most types of ichthyosis are congenital. Common congenital subtypes include ichthyosis vulgaris, X-linked ichthyosis, lamellar ichthyosis, epidermolytic hyperkeratosis, harlequin-type ichthyosis, Netherton syndrome, and Sjögren-Larsson syndrome. Ethnicity does not appear to influence the prevalence of ichthyosis. In domestic dogs, ichthyosis of varying severity has been documented in certain breeds, including Golden Retrievers, American Bulldogs, Jack Russell Terriers, and Cairn Terriers. The clinical presentation of ichthyosis includes symptoms such as dry skin, scaly skin, and thickened skin. On physical examination, the skin appears dry and scaly, with findings consistent with ichthyosis vulgaris. Diagnosis can be confirmed through a skin biopsy. Treatment for ichthyosis primarily involves the use of topical creams and emollient oils to hydrate the skin. Retinoids may be prescribed for certain subtypes. Sunlight exposure can have variable effects, either improving or exacerbating the condition. Ocular complications, such as corneal and ocular surface diseases, may occur. Vascularizing keratitis, particularly in congenital keratitis-ichthyosis-deafness (KID) syndrome, can worsen with isotretinoin therapy. Ectropion, if present, can be managed surgically after adequate skin hydration. Currently, there is no known method to prevent ichthyosis.
